If the qword at module address 0x750 is still zero, RDX is stored there and the qwords at [RDX+0x60] and [RDX+0x58] are cached at 0x740 and 0x748; otherwise the pointer already at 0x740 is reused. It then calls through offset 0x50 of that pointer with arguments (0x200, 8, 0x4C0, 0, address of RSP+0x50) and, if the result is not negative, through offset 0xA8 with (0x6C0, the first out value, address of RSP+0x58). The structure those two offsets belong to is not identified by this listing, so no UEFI service name is claimed for either call.

name: module_entry_scan_and_apply
comment: The PE entry point: saves RBX, calls 0x0000032c and then 0x00000438 with the two incoming arguments (RCX and RDX) passed through unchanged, and returns without setting a status of its own, so what it returns is the 0 that 0x00000438 leaves in RAX. Neither call's result is inspected.

name: module_entry
comment: Module entry point: saves RBX, allocates 32 bytes of stack and calls 0x32c and then 0x438 with the incoming RCX and RDX unchanged, restoring the stack and RBX before returning. The return value of the second call is discarded.

name: read_timestamp_counter
comment: Executes RDTSC, shifts RDX left by 32 and ORs it into RAX, so RAX holds the 64-bit timestamp counter on return and RDX is clobbered. Both call sites in this module (0x3F4 and 0x414, both in the routine at 0x36C) discard the value.

name: disable_interrupts
comment: Executes CLI, clearing the interrupt-enable flag, and returns immediately.

name: module_entry_point
comment: Takes the second UEFI argument as a system table pointer, calls 0x384, and on the first call caches that pointer at 0xe70 together with system table offset +0x60 at 0xe60 and +0x58 at 0xe68. It then makes an indirect call through the cached table pointer at offset 0x170 with the constants 0x200, 8, 0x4ac, 0, 0xda0 and a 16-byte stack buffer; which UEFI service sits at that table offset is not identified in this repository.

name: module_entry_forward
comment: Module entry point: saves RDX in RBX, calls 0x32C, then reloads RDX and calls 0x438. Neither callee reads the first argument (RCX), so the entry image handle is not used anywhere in this module. It returns the value 0x438 leaves in RAX, which that function zeroes.

name: module_entry
comment: Reserves 0x28 bytes of shadow space, calls 0x324 with both incoming arguments untouched, then calls 0x430 without setting up any arguments for it, restores RSP and returns. EAX is 0 on return because 0x430 ends in XOR EAX,EAX. Nothing here touches an I/O port or a setup variable directly.

name: module_entry
comment: Saves RDX, subtracts 0x20 from RSP, calls 0x32C and then 0x438 with the same two arguments it was given, restores RSP and RBX, and returns without setting a return value. Between them the two callees are the whole of what the module does: a configuration-table GUID search plus a timed interrupts-disabled wait (0x32C), then an EC read, two variable writes and a write to I/O port 0xCF9 (0x438).

name: module_entry
comment: The module entry point, which Ghidra already calls entry. It pushes RBX, allocates 0x20 bytes of stack, calls 0x32C with the incoming RCX and RDX unchanged, then restores RDX from RBX and calls 0x438 with the same two arguments; EAX is left as 0x438 left it and the 0x438 result is not inspected.

name: module_entry_register_signal_event
comment: The module entry point. It calls 0x00000388 with both incoming register arguments unchanged, then, if the global at 0x00000c70 is still zero, caches its second argument there along with the qwords at [RDX+0x60] and [RDX+0x58] at 0x00000c60 and 0x00000c68; offsets 0x58 and 0x60 are where RuntimeServices and BootServices sit in EFI_SYSTEM_TABLE. It then calls the entry at offset 0x170 of 0x00000c60 with the six values 0x200, 8, 0x00000494, 0, 0x00000bc0 and RSP+0x50, the first five of which match CreateEventEx's Type, NotifyTPL, NotifyFunction, NotifyContext and Event out-parameter, so the event is stored through 0x00000bc0 with 0x00000494 as its notify function. The call's status is discarded and 0 is returned.

name: module_entry_point
comment: The module entry point. It saves RDX, calls 0x0000032c with both incoming arguments unchanged, discards that call's result, reloads RDX from the saved copy and calls 0x00000438, then restores the stack and returns 0x00000438's RAX. It never reads its first argument.

name: module_init_entry
comment: Pushes RBX, reserves a 0x20-byte frame, and calls two routines in order with the second incoming argument still in RDX: 0x32C first, then 0x438, with the first incoming argument (RCX) passed to 0x438. The PE entry signature the module was built against is not decoded here; only the two call targets and their argument passing are visible.

name: module_entry
comment: The module entry point, called with the system table pointer in RDX. It calls 0x388 first, then, only while the global 0xB50 is still null, saves RDX there along with the Boot Services pointer at [RDX+0x60] in 0xB40 and the Runtime Services pointer at [RDX+0x58] in 0xB48; on a later call it reloads 0xB40 instead. It then calls the Boot Services entry at offset 0x170 (gBS->CreateEventEx) with type 0x200, notify type 0x10, notify function 0x494, notify context 0, the 16-byte group pointer at 0xAB0 and a stack buffer at RSP+0x50 for the created event, and returns 0 without looking at the result.

name: module_entry_scan_and_init_variable
comment: Saves the second argument, calls the table scan at 0x348, then - only while the global at 0xBF8 is still zero - stores that argument in 0xBF8 and the qword at its offset 0x58 in 0xBF0, and calls 0x454. EAX is zeroed after that call, so the module entry returns 0 whatever 0x454 returns. The second argument is the pointer whose offsets 0x60, 0x68 and 0x70 the callees use, the array at 0x70 being walked in 0x18-byte steps.

name: module_entry
comment: The module entry point, which Ghidra already calls entry. It pushes RBX, allocates 0x20 bytes of stack, calls 0x0000032C with the incoming RCX and RDX unchanged, then restores RDX from RBX and calls 0x00000438 - without restoring RCX, so 0x00000438's first argument is whatever 0x0000032C left in RCX - and returns with RAX as 0x00000438 set it. Nothing in either callee touches a USB controller, a HID report or any address this repository documents, so the module name is not corroborated by the code.

name: module_init_entry
comment: The module entry point, which Ghidra already names entry. It saves the second incoming argument in RBX, reserves 0x20 bytes of stack, and calls 0x32C and then 0x438, each with the first argument still in RCX and the second in RDX: 0x32C reads only RDX, and 0x438 spills RCX to a stack slot without ever reading it. 0x438 returns 0 in RAX on its only exit, so this entry returns 0; the entry signature the module was built against is not decoded here.

name: cpuid_read
comment: One unconditional CPUID: the leaf in RCX is moved into EAX, and each result register is written out only when the corresponding pointer is non-NULL - EAX to param_2 (RDX), EBX to param_3 (R8), EDX to param_5 (the fifth stack argument) and ECX, which still holds the leaf, to param_4 (R9). The decompiled C instead shows a switch over the leaf dispatching to helpers named cpuid_basic_info, cpuid_brand_part1_info and a dozen others; none of those calls exist in the listing.

name: cpu_pause
comment: One pause instruction and a return. It is the spin primitive the 0x1808 polling loops at 0x364 and 0x1EE4 call once per turn.

name: enable_interrupts
comment: A single STI followed by RET, which clears the interrupt-disable flag. The routine at 0x36C calls it at 0x41D to restore the interrupt state it captured before its port-wait loop.

name: read_rflags
comment: Pushes the flags register and pops it into RAX, returning the EFLAGS image as it stood just before the call.

name: enable_interrupts
comment: Executes sti and returns. 0x37C calls it only when the flags it read earlier had bit 9 set, so the interrupt-enable flag ends up back where the cli in that function left it.

name: memset_bytes
comment: memset: destination RCX, fill byte in DL, count in R8. RAX takes the count and RDI the destination, then xchg RDX,RCX puts the fill byte in RCX for stosb.rep while leaving the original destination in RDX, which is moved to RAX before the return. The decompiled C reads the count and the fill byte the other way round; the register shuffling settles it. Only the low byte of the second argument is stored.

name: scan_record_list_and_register_notify
comment: Stores the pointer from the incoming second argument at 0x8D0 and the qword at [arg2+0x60] at 0x8D8, then calls 0x764 twice and walks the list that call returns: a run of variable-length records whose first 16-bit word is a type and whose second is a length, ending at a 0xFFFF sentinel, and a record of type 0x4 whose qwords at +0x8 and +0x10 match the module constants at 0x8A0 and 0x8A8 takes the exit branch. If no such record is reached it samples RFLAGS, executes CLI, waits 0x16B counts of the 24-bit counter read from I/O port 0x1808 (spinning through 0x260), and then restores the sampled interrupt-enable bit with STI or CLI. The exit calls the function pointer at [0x8D8+0x140] with the arguments 0x890, 0 and the address 0x8E8, and on a non-negative result calls the first qword of what that wrote at 0x8E8 with the argument 0x8F0; what that table at [arg2+0x60] is, and the meaning of 0x890/0x8E8/0x8F0, are not decoded here.

name: init_scan_records_and_install
comment: Caches [arg2+0x60] at 0xdb0 and arg2 itself at 0xda8, calls the table lookup at 0xa70 twice, then walks the record array it returns: each record has a 16-bit type word at +0 and a 16-bit size at +2, and the loop compares the type against 4 and 0xffff and the two qwords at +8 and +0x10 against the qwords at 0xd60 and 0xd68. If the matching record is found it jumps straight to 0x3e9; otherwise it saves RFLAGS, executes CLI, polls I/O port 0x1808 (masked to 24 bits) until 0x16b counts have elapsed while calling the pause helper at 0x2c0, and finally restores the saved IF state with STI or CLI. The tail at 0x3e9 calls [0xdb0+0x140] with (0xd30, 0, 0xdd8) and, if the result is non-negative, calls the first function pointer stored at 0xdd8 with (that pointer, 0xde0); what these table entries are is not established in this module.

name: lookup_record_table_and_invoke
comment: Stores the caller's second argument at 0x00000D80 and the qword at [arg+0x60] at 0x00000D88, then walks the record array that 0x00000A9C returns: each record has a 16-bit type at +0, a 16-bit stride to the next record at +2, and qwords at +8 and +0x10, with type 0xFFFF ending the walk. A type-4 record whose two qwords match those at 0x00000D20 and 0x00000D28 jumps straight to the tail call; when the walk finds nothing, the flags word is saved, CLI runs, the 24-bit counter at I/O port 0x1808 is spun with PAUSE until it has advanced 0x16B (the TSC read inside that loop has its result discarded), and STI or CLI is issued according to bit 9 (IF) of the saved flags. Both paths then call the pointer at offset 0x140 of the table at 0x00000D88 with (0xD10, 0, &0x00000DA8, 0xFFFF) and, if the result is not negative, call the qword at *0x00000DA8 with (0x00000DA8, 0x00000DB0).

name: init_match_record_and_call_iface
comment: Caches its second argument at global 0xF48 and that argument's field at offset 0x60 at global 0xF50, calls the 0xC38 lookup twice (the second call returns the cached value), then walks a variable-length record table starting at the returned pointer: each record has a 16-bit type at +0 and a 16-bit stride at +2 that is added to the pointer, and the walk ends at a 0xFFFF type word. A record is a match if its type is 4 and its qwords at +8 and +0x10 equal the globals at 0xEE0 and 0xEE8; a match jumps straight to 0x3E9, and a terminator with no match falls into the delay path. The delay path busy-waits on I/O port 0x1808 until the counter's low 24 bits have advanced 0x16B (calling the PAUSE stub 0x260 each iteration), reads RFLAGS through 0x2A0, and restores interrupts with STI or CLI according to bit 9. Finally, if the pointer at global 0xF78 is null it calls the pointer at offset 0x140 of the table at 0xF50 with (0xEC0, 0, the address of 0xF78) and, on a non-negative status, calls the first vtable entry of the interface it returns with (0xF78, 0xF80); the offset 0x140 matches no documented BootServices slot, so that service is not named here.

name: scan_table_for_matching_record
comment: Caches [RDX+0x60] at 0xA98 and RDX itself at 0xA90, then calls 0x7C4 twice (the first return value is discarded) and walks the pointer the second returns: a u16 type at offset 0 of each record and a u16 size at offset 2 that advances the cursor, a type of 0xFFFF ending the walk, and a type of 4 whose qwords at +0x8 and +0x10 equal the module constants at 0xA60 and 0xA68 jumping to the common tail. Reaching the 0xFFFF end instead runs a second path that saves IF via 0x300, calls 0x2F0, reads the 24-bit counter at I/O port 0x1808, and spins through 0x2C0 until (base + 0x16B - value) has bit 23 set, then restores IF with 0x2E0 or 0x2F0. At 0x3E9 it calls the pointer at offset 0x140 of the structure cached at 0xA98 with arguments (0xA50, 0, &global 0xAB8) and, if that return is non-negative, calls the pointer stored at 0xAB8 with argument 0xAC0; which UEFI service the 0x140 entry is has not been decoded.

name: read_tsc
comment: Executes rdtsc, shifts RDX left 32 and ORs it into RAX, so it returns the 64-bit time-stamp counter. Its only caller in this module is 0x364, which calls it twice and discards both results, so what the module wants the timestamp for is not decoded here.

name: disable_interrupts
comment: A single CLI followed by RET, which sets the interrupt-disable flag. The routine at 0x36C calls it at 0x3DB immediately after capturing RFLAGS, and again at 0x424 when the captured IF bit was clear.

name: disable_interrupts
comment: Executes cli and returns. 0x37C calls it before its port-0x1808 busy wait, and calls it again afterwards when the flags read at the start showed bit 9 clear.

name: build_adas_record_and_call_services
comment: On the first call only it caches the second parameter in 0x8F8 and copies [param2+0x60] to 0x8E8 and [param2+0x58] to 0x8F0. It then calls the function at [qword 0x8D8]+0x40 with (0xA, 0x10, 0x900), the third argument being the address of a module global, and returns that call's result unchanged if it is negative. Otherwise it zeroes the 16 bytes at the pointer stored in 0x900, writes the ASCII 'ADAS' there, the low 32 bits of that pointer as a dword at offset 5 and 0x10 as a word at offset 9, then calls [qword 0x8D8]+0x148 with (&local copy of param1, 0x870, 0x900, 0) and [qword 0x8D8]+0x170 with (0x200, 8, 0x41C, 0, 0x860, &local buffer) and returns 0. What the three table services at offsets 0x40, 0x148 and 0x170 are is not established here.

name: enable_interrupts
comment: A single sti followed by a return, setting IF in RFLAGS. 0x364 calls it only when the IF bit it had read through 0x360 was set, so it restores the interrupt-enable state the module had just cleared with 0x350.

name: read_rflags
comment: Pushes the flags register and pops it into RAX, so RFLAGS is returned in RAX. The routine at 0x36C calls it at 0x3D3, then disables interrupts and keeps bit 9 (IF) in BL to decide whether to re-enable them after the wait.

name: read_eflags
comment: pushfq then pop RAX, returning the current flags register. Its only caller (0x37C) keeps bit 9 of the result and re-enables interrupts if that bit was set.

name: memset_zero_bytes
comment: Zeroes length bytes at the RCX destination: RAX is cleared, RDI takes the pointer, and length>>3 plus length&7 drive stosq.rep followed by stosb.rep, so there is no caller-supplied fill byte. The return value in RAX is the destination as it was on entry, restored by the pop of the register pushed at 0x341.

name: scan_tag_table_then_call_protocol
comment: Caches the qword at [RDX+0x60] in 0xBE8 and RDX itself in 0xBE0, calls 0x8E8 twice (the first call caches the pointer, so the second is redundant) and walks the pointer it returns as an array of records with a 16-bit tag at +0, a 16-bit stride at +2 and a 16-byte identifier at +8: a record is compared against the bytes at 0xB90 and 0xB98, a tag of 0xFFFF ends the walk, and a match skips the rest. If the list ends without a match it takes the other branch instead: read the flags, CLI, then spin on I/O port 0x1808 until its low 24 bits have advanced 0x16B past the first sample, and finally STI or CLI according to the saved interrupt-enable bit. Both branches converge: when the global at 0xC08 is zero it calls [0xBE8+0x140] with (0xB70, 0, 0xC08) and, on a non-negative result, calls the qword at [0xC08] with (0xC08, 0xC10).

name: disable_interrupts
comment: A single cli followed by a return, clearing IF in RFLAGS. 0x364 calls it before its 0x1808 polling loop and again afterwards when the IF bit it had saved was clear.

name: module_entry
comment: The module entry point, which Ghidra already calls entry. It saves RDX, calls 0x36C with the incoming RDX, restores RDX and calls 0x478, then returns without writing RAX, so the status left in RAX by 0x478 is what the module returns.

name: module_entry
comment: The module entry point: saves RBX, calls 0x37C with the two incoming arguments and then 0x4A4 with the same pair, and returns whatever 0x4A4 left in RAX without testing it.

name: read_flags
comment: pushfq, pop RAX, return: hands the caller's RFLAGS back unchanged. 0x364 keeps the result and tests bit 9 (IF) to choose between 0x340 and 0x350 once its polling loop is done.

name: overclock_module_entry
comment: Module entry (Ghidra's `entry`). It saves the tables the system table in RDX points at: BootServices from [RDX+0x60] to 0x2690, RuntimeServices from [RDX+0x58] to 0x2698, and the system table pointer itself to 0x2688. It calls 0x1E28 (a configuration-table lookup) and then 0x1E94, and only when 0x1E94 leaves RAX zero does it read the flags, clear interrupts, sample 16-bit I/O port 0x1808, and spin until (((sample & 0xFFFFFF) + 0x16B) - next sample) has bit 0x17 set, calling the pause at 0x320 each turn, before re-enabling or leaving interrupts off per the saved IF and calling 0x400.

name: cache_system_table_and_locate_protocol
comment: Entry-time setup: it caches the incoming RDX at 0x14E0 and [RDX+0x60] at 0x14E8, calls 0x1118 twice, and uses the first result as the base of a 24-byte-record walk that compares each record's first word against 0xFFFF (stop, then treated as not-found) and 4 (candidate), takes the stride from the second word, and matches the qwords at +8 and +0x10 against the 16 bytes at 0x13F8/0x1400. On no match it captures RFLAGS, runs 0x330, waits on I/O port 0x1808 until the 24-bit value there has advanced 0x16B ticks, reads the timestamp counter, and restores interrupts with 0x320 or 0x330 according to the captured IF bit. Whether or not a record matched, it then calls the boot-services entry at offset 0x140 (argument shape of LocateProtocol) with the GUID at 0x13D0 and an interface pointer stored at 0x1510, and calls the first method of the returned interface with (This, 0x1518). 0x1118 returns a pointer to a matched configuration-table entry's third qword (entry+0x10), which is what this walk starts from, and the module data at 0x13B0, 0x13D0 and 0x13F8 is not in the listing, so neither the record type nor the protocol is identified here.

name: entry_dispatch
comment: The module entry point, which Ghidra already names entry. It calls 0x39C with the incoming RCX and RDX unchanged, then 0x4B8 with the same two arguments, and returns without propagating either status.

name: walk_typed_table_for_guid
comment: Caches the second argument at 0x13B0 and its +0x60 field at 0x13B8, calls 0x1054 twice, then walks the pointer it returns: entries with a 16-bit type word at +0 and a 16-bit stride at +2, ended by type 0xFFFF. A type-4 entry whose 8-byte fields at +8 and +0x10 match the two halves of the values at 0x1348/0x1350 skips the wait; otherwise the function reads the flags, cli's, spins on port 0x1808 until (first 24-bit read + 0x16B) minus a later read no longer has bit 23 set, and restores the interrupt flag. Both paths then obtain the interface at 0x13E0 through the table at 0x13B8+0x140 (arguments 0x1300, 0, and the interface slot), call the first function pointer of that interface with (interface, 0x13E8), and tail-call the same table entry with (0x12D0, 0, 0x13F0). The layout of the second argument and the identity of the two values it points at are not established by this listing.

name: cpu_pause
comment: A single PAUSE instruction followed by ret. Nothing is read, written, compared or branched on.

name: init_module_and_locate_guids
comment: Caches system table +0x60 at 0xe58 and the table pointer itself at 0xe50, calls 0xb34 twice to resolve a cached table pointer, then walks a record table: it reads a 16-bit tag at +0x0, uses the 16-bit field at +0x2 as the stride to the next record, stops on tag 0xffff or tag 4, and compares the 8-byte fields at +0x8 and +0x10 against the two constants read from 0xdf0 and 0xdf8 (the tag sentinel 0xffff is loaded into R9W). On a match it skips straight to the protocol section; only on the no-match path does it run the 0x1808 delay loop with interrupts enabled or disabled according to bit 9 of the saved flags. It then makes an indirect call through the cached table at offset 0x140 with (GUID at 0xdd0, 0, out-pointer 0xe80) and, if a handle is present, calls its first method with 0xe88 as the argument, before tail-calling the same offset 0x140 with (GUID at 0xdb0, 0, 0xe90).

name: scan_for_record_then_locate_protocol
comment: Called from the module entry with the system table pointer in RDX, it saves the Boot Services pointer read at [RDX+0x60] in the global 0xB38 and RDX itself in 0xB30, then calls the configuration-table lookup at 0x840 twice, discarding the first result. From the pointer that lookup returns it walks a record chain, advancing by the 16-bit value at +2 of the current record, and stops at a record whose first 16-bit word is 4 and whose qwords at +8 and +0x10 equal the constants at 0xAE0 and 0xAE8; a first word of 0xFFFF ends the walk with no match. On the no-match path it clears interrupts, records the 24-bit value read from I/O port 0x1808, spins through the PAUSE helper at 0x2C0 until 0x16B ticks have passed, and restores the interrupt flag to what bit 9 of the flags it read held. Both paths then call the Boot Services entry at offset 0x140 (gBS->LocateProtocol) for the 16 bytes at 0xAC0 into the global 0xB60 and, on a non-negative result, call the returned interface's first function with 0xB68 as its argument; none of the 16-byte values in the data area is decoded here.

name: read_timestamp_counter
comment: Executes RDTSC, shifts the EDX half left by 32 and ORs it into EAX, returning the 64-bit cycle count. At both call sites in this module, both in the entry, the returned value is discarded and the instruction is used only for its serializing effect.

name: init_locate_protocol
comment: Saves the second argument at 0x1350 and the qword at [arg2+0x60] at 0x1358, calls 0x1040 twice keeping only the second result as a record pointer, then walks that record chain: the word at +0 is a type, the word at +2 is the stride to the next record, 0xFFFF ends the walk, and a type-4 record is matched against the 16 bytes at 0x1300/0x1308. On a match, or at the end of the walk, it fetches an interface through [0x1358]+0x140 with the GUID at 0x12D0, calls the first method of the returned interface with (interface, &0x1388), and tail-calls 0xFE0 with the GUID at 0x12E0. If no type-4 record matched it instead takes the flags at 0x320, executes CLI at 0x310, captures the interrupt-enable bit, and spins on I/O port 0x1808 until bit 23 of (base+0x16B - a fresh read) is set before restoring the flag with 0x300 or 0x310. Which services the +0x140 slot and the returned interface belong to is not identified here.

name: enable_interrupts_sti
comment: A single STI followed by ret: sets the interrupt-enable flag and returns immediately, without saving or restoring any state.

name: cpuid_read_leaf
comment: cpuid wrapper taking the leaf in ECX and the subleaf in EDX, then distributing the four results through optional output pointers: ECX - the value cpuid itself returned, i.e. the maximum leaf - to the fifth argument, EAX to R8, EBX to R9 and EDX to the sixth argument, each store skipped when its pointer is zero. The leaf is left in EAX and is what the function returns. Both stack destinations are read at RSP+0x38 and RSP+0x40, which with two pushes are entry+0x28 and entry+0x30, so they are the fifth and sixth arguments rather than shadow.

name: disable_interrupts_cli
comment: A single CLI followed by ret: clears the interrupt-enable flag and returns immediately, without saving or restoring any state.

name: read_rflags
comment: PUSHFQ then POP RAX, returning the 64-bit RFLAGS value in RAX. Only RFLAGS bit 9 (the interrupt-enable flag) is examined by its one caller; the remaining bits, including the arithmetic and direction flags, are discarded.

The module's own entry point, which Ghidra already calls `entry`; the hand-written restatement names it as "the module entry" and names no symbol for it, so this row carries the address and the comment and leaves the name alone. It dispatches through the library constructors at 0x3EC into OemOcDxeMain (0x4F8).

The "library constructors" of the hand-written restatement: the static-init chain that resolves gRT and gST before the module body runs. The restatement names them in prose and gives them no symbol, so again the row carries the address only.

name: memset_words
comment: 16-bit memset: destination RCX, fill word in DX, count in R8. RAX takes the count, RDI the destination, and xchg RDX,RCX puts the fill word in RCX for stosw.rep, leaving the original destination in RDX for the return in RAX. stosw stores AX, so only the low 16 bits of the second argument reach memory, and the count is used as given with no zero check.

name: cpu_pause
comment: A single pause instruction followed by ret - the spin-wait primitive the module's polling loops call. It takes no arguments, reads and writes no memory, and returns with whatever the caller had in RAX.

name: read_state_byte_and_send_commands
comment: Reads a config byte from absolute address 0xFF430035 into DIL and issues three controller writes on the 0x62 data / 0x66 status port pair: 0x648 with command 0xA3 and data 0x07, 0x648 with command 0xA2 and data 0x8C, and 0x4E4 with command 0xA4. It then polls the status byte at port 0x66 until bit 0 is set (bounded by 0x20000 iterations of the 15-unit delay at 0x830) and reads one byte from port 0x62; that byte has bit 0 cleared when DIL is 0, set when DIL is 1, and is not sent at all for any other DIL, and it is passed to 0x710 in R9B. The failure paths and the poll timeout converge at 0x4B6, where the byte used is instead the low byte of the incoming RDX, which the module entry at 0x310 never initialises. Returns 0 unconditionally.

name: read_tsc
comment: Executes rdtsc and returns the 64-bit counter in RAX: the EDX half is shifted left by 0x20 and OR'd in. No serialising instruction brackets the read, so the value is not ordered against earlier stores; callers use it only to burn a measured interval.

name: apply_platform_port_registers
comment: On its first call it caches RDX in 0x00000e08 and the qwords at [RDX+0x60] and [RDX+0x58] in 0x00000df8 and 0x00000e00, then reads the six fixed bytes at 0xFF430004, 0xFF430005, 0xFF430006, 0xFF430007, 0xFF430008 and 0xFF43000A. If the bytes at 0xFF430006, 0xFF430007 and 0xFF430008 are not 0xFF it writes them through 0x00000a14 as register bytes 0x6C, 0x6D and 0x6E. If the byte at 0xFF43000A is not 0xFF it reads register byte 0x66 into a zeroed stack byte, writes the byte at 0xFF430004 as register byte 0x65, writes that stack byte AND 0xE0 OR the byte at 0xFF430005 as register byte 0x66, and finally calls 0x0000053c and returns 0. What the fixed bytes at 0xFF430004-0xFF43000A hold and what register bytes 0x65, 0x66, 0x6C-0x6E select is not decoded here; 0x00000a14 and 0x00000a74 ignore their first two arguments.

name: init_register_two_callbacks
comment: If [0xdc8] is zero it caches arg2 at 0xdc8, [arg2+0x60] at 0xdb8 and [arg2+0x58] at 0xdc0, otherwise it reuses the cached [0xdb8]. It then makes two six-argument calls through [0xdb8+0x170] with (0x200, 0x10, 0x570, 0, &0xd20, &stack_0x50) and (0x200, 0x10, 0x4e4, 0, &0xd50, &stack_0x40) - the argument shape of UEFI CreateEventEx, with the module's own code RVAs 0x570 and 0x4e4 in the callback slot - and returns 0 without testing either result. The identity of the table at [arg2+0x60] is not established in this module.

name: read_modify_write_two_variables
comment: On the first entry it caches the second parameter in 0x838 and [param2+0x58] in 0x830, otherwise it reloads 0x830. It calls the table entry at +0x48 (the GetVariable offset in the standard EFI_RUNTIME_SERVICES layout) twice, for the names 0x7d0 and 0x7e0, each with a 16-byte GUID constant built in the frame ({0xec87d643,0x4bb5eba4,0x3e3fe5a1,0xa90db236} and {0xd1405d16,0x46957afc,0x454112bb,0xa295369d}), a shared data-size slot at RBP+0x750, a data-pointer slot preset to 0x7d8 and to 8 respectively, and a pointer to an attributes slot, returning 0 immediately if either call returns a negative status. It then reads the byte at RBP+0x6ab: if it is 1 and the byte at RBP+0x6a2 is also 1 it stores 1 at RBP+0x760 and RBP+0x69c, if it is 1 and that byte differs it stores 0 and 2 respectively, and if it is 0 it stores 0 in both slots. Finally it calls the entry at +0x58 (SetVariable) once per name, passing as the data size the low dword of the shared slot at RBP+0x750 and as the data the pointer each +0x48 call left in that variable's data-pointer slot, and always returns 0; the significance of the two variable names and their GUIDs is not decoded here.

name: program_indexed_ports_by_flags
comment: On its first call caches RDX at 0xAA8 and [RDX+0x58] at 0xAA0. It reads one byte from memory address 0x00FF43000F, writes that byte to I/O port 0x71 after selecting index 0x7D through port 0x70, and returns 0 at once if the byte was 0xFF. Bit 0 of the byte drives a poll of port 0x66 until bit 1 clears (capped at 0x20000 iterations) followed by a write of 0x7C to 0x66; bit 1 drives calls to the 0x62/0x66/0x80 helpers at 0x6FC and 0x598, with index bytes 0xA3, 0xA2, 0xA4 and 0xA5 and data bytes 0x04, 0x9F and the byte read back from port 0x62 with bit 0 forced set, finishing with 0x79 and 0x9F written through ports 0x70/0x71; bit 6 writes 0x7A then 0x01 through 0x70/0x71. If either of the two 0x6FC calls before the 0xA5 write fails, or a poll times out, the value sent in that write is taken from the first incoming argument instead of from the port read. Always returns 0.

name: rewrite_nv_variable_gated_on_byte_44
comment: On its first call caches RDX at 0x788 and [RDX+0x58] at 0x780, builds a 16-byte value on the stack (F1B77045 E8AD4949 8DC34064 72842384), and calls the entry at offset 0x48 of 0x780 with (0x730, &guid, &attributes at RBP+0x650, &size at RBP+0x660, &data at RSP+0x40), the size pre-set to 0x6F2. Those five arguments and the EFI_STATUS return match GetVariable's signature, and the second call passes the same name, GUID, attributes, size and data to the entry at offset 0x58 of 0x780, matching SetVariable, but the code names no variable and the bytes at 0x730 are not in the listings. If the first call returns non-negative and byte 0x44 of the returned data (address RBP-0x7C, inside the data buffer and not the attributes slot) equals 1, it zeroes data+0x21E and data+0x22A and calls the 0x58 entry, writing the modified buffer back with the attributes and size the first call stored; the meaning of the gated byte is not decoded here. Returns 0 in RAX on every path.

name: enable_interrupts
comment: sti followed by ret. It sets IF in RFLAGS, enabling maskable interrupts, and returns immediately with no other effect on the machine.

name: disable_interrupts
comment: cli followed by ret. It clears IF in RFLAGS, disabling maskable interrupts, and returns immediately with no other effect on the machine.

name: rdrand_store_u64
comment: Executes rdrand and branches on the carry flag. On failure (CF clear) it zeroes RAX, returns 0 and writes no memory; on success it stores the 64-bit value through the RCX pointer and returns 1 in EAX.

name: signal_notify_update_variables_and_registers
comment: Reads two runtime variables through GetVariable at offset 0x48 of 0x00000c68, the 16-byte names at 0x00000c00/0x00000ba0 into a 0x7d8-byte buffer and 0x00000c10/0x00000be0 into a 0xb4-byte buffer, returning the first negative status. If byte 0x2f of the second buffer is 0xff it replaces it with 1 when the byte at fixed memory 0xff430034 is 0x22 or 0x24 and with 0 otherwise, reads port register byte 0x9f through 0x0000089c, and writes both buffers back through SetVariable at offset 0x58 with the second buffer's only change being that byte. It then makes three port exchanges through 0x000007d4 on the 0x62 channel, 0xa3 with 0x07 then 0xa2 with 0x51 then 0xa5 with a byte derived from the flag (0xa0 for 0, 0x00 for 1, 0x10 for 2, and the uninitialised stack byte at RBP+0x810 for any other value), stopping at the first negative status, and finally reads register byte 0x51 back through 0x0000089c into that same stack slot and discards the result. It returns the status of the first SetVariable, or of the first GetVariable on the early exits; what the two variable names select is not decoded here.

name: entry
comment: The module entry point, which Ghidra already calls entry. It saves RBX, keeps the two incoming arguments in RDI and RBX across the first call, calls 0x000004dc with them, restores them into RCX and RDX, calls 0x00000c6c, and returns without inspecting either result.

name: init_allocate_and_register
comment: If 0x1370 is still zero it caches the second argument at 0x1370, [arg2+0x60] at 0x1360 and [arg2+0x58] at 0x1368. It then calls [0x1358]+0x40 with (0xA, 0x112, &0x1398); a negative result is returned unchanged, and a non-negative one is followed by zeroing 0x112 bytes at the pointer stored in 0x1398 through 0x260, a call to [0x1358]+0x148 with (&stack copy of arg1, 0x12A0, 0x1398, 0) whose result is discarded, and a call to [0x1358]+0x170 with (0x200, 8, 0x57C, 0, 0x1290, &stack out-slot), after which it returns 0. The three callees are reached through saved table slots rather than named symbols, so which services they are is not decoded here.

name: lookup_table_entry
comment: RCX points at a 16-byte key and RDX at an output slot. The output is cleared to 0, a count is read from [0x730 + 0x68] and an array pointer from [0x730 + 0x70], and 0x18-byte records are scanned with each record's first two qwords compared against the key; on a match the record's third qword (record + 0x10) is stored through the output slot and 0 is returned. If the count is 0 or no record matches, the output stays 0 and 0x800000000000000E (EFI_NOT_FOUND) is returned. The structure behind 0x730 and the meaning of the 16-byte key are not identified further by this listing.

name: find_name_tag_record
comment: Computes the NUL-terminated length of the string in the third parameter, builds a 4-byte key on the stack from the constant 0x5F5F5F5F overwritten with those bytes by the copy at 0x7A0, and scans the buffer in the first parameter at 4-byte stride for the count in the second parameter, comparing each dword against the key. On a hit it tests the byte at match-1 against 0x5C and 0x5E and the byte before that against 0x08; when both hold it fills the caller's record with the values RAX-1, RAX, match+4, 3 and 0 at offsets 0x00, 0x08, 0x10, 0x18 and 0x1C and returns 0, otherwise it resumes the same scan at match+4 with the count reduced by the number of dwords already passed. A scan that runs out returns 0x800000000000000E, and the fourth parameter is saved to the stack and never read.

name: write_controller_command_byte
comment: Selects a status/command port - 0x64 when the first argument is 0x60, otherwise 0x66 - and polls it until bit 1 (input buffer full) is clear, calling 0x830 with 15 on each iteration. It then OUTs the second argument to that same port. Returns 0 on success or 0x8000000000000007 if the bit has not cleared after 0x20000 iterations.

name: OemOcDxeMain
comment: What this module decides on every boot: (1) EC 0x0741 bit 7 set -> overclocking recovery: turn CpuSetup's "OverClocking Feature" off, raise UniWillVariable.OverClockRecoveryFlag, clear the EC bit. (2) otherwise -> copy UniWillVariable.MemoryOverClockSwitch into Setup[0x7D7], which is the byte that un-suppresses the "Memory" (Memory Overclocking Menu) link on the vendor Advanced page; if the switch is 1 and OC is enabled, drive PCH pad GPP_B22's TX state high; and copy the Control Center's CPU core-voltage values into CpuSetup. EC_0741_OC_RECOVERY is BIT7 of that byte; bit 0 of the same byte is "AP exist". Reached from the module entry at 0x3D0 through the library constructors at 0x3EC. The byte is seeded from the low byte of ImageHandle and only overwritten if the EC read succeeds, so a failed read tests an uninitialised value (as decompiled; not observed).

name: find_config_table_entry_by_guid
comment: Returns the pointer cached at 0x790 when it is non-zero. Otherwise it zeroes that global and walks the array whose element count is at [0x770+0x68] and whose base is at [0x770+0x70] in 0x18-byte steps, comparing the first two qwords of each entry against the 16 bytes at 0x700 and 0x708; on a match it caches and returns the third qword of the entry, at +0x10, and it returns 0 when the count is zero or nothing matches. Offsets 0x68 and 0x70 are where NumberOfTableEntries and ConfigurationTable sit in EFI_SYSTEM_TABLE, consistent with 0x32C using [param+0x60] as a service table and 0x438 using [param+0x58]; the 16 bytes searched for at 0x700 and 0x708 are not identified here.

name: get_cached_table_pointer
comment: If the qword at module address 0x758 is zero it calls the routine at 0x4CC with the 16-byte key at 0x6D0 and 0x758 as the output slot, then returns the qword at 0x758. The lookup result is therefore cached from the first call onward, and a failed lookup leaves 0 in the slot and returns 0.

name: drain_controller_output_to_port_80
comment: Selects a status port (0x64 when the argument is 0x60, else 0x66) and a data port (0x60 or 0x62 correspondingly). While the status byte has bit 0 (output buffer full) set it reads the data port and writes that byte to I/O port 0x80 - the destination is computed as data_port+2+0x1E, so it is 0x80 on both selections - then calls 0x830 with 5000 before re-reading the status. Returns 0 or 0x8000000000000007 after 0x20000 iterations.

name: write_command_port_byte
comment: Picks port 0x64 when the first byte argument is 0x60 and port 0x66 otherwise, polls that port until bit 1 reads as zero (calling 0x890 with 15 between polls, capped at 0x20000 iterations), then writes the second byte argument to the same port. Returns 0 on success or 0x8000000000000007 if the cap is hit.

name: write_value_by_type_byte
comment: Calls 0x4D8 to locate the record for the name string in the third parameter and returns its status unchanged if it is negative. A leading byte of 0x0A, 0x0B, 0x0C or 0x0E makes it store the fourth parameter at record+1 as 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes respectively and return 0; a leading byte of 0 or 1 instead writes the fourth parameter into the leading byte itself, and only when that parameter is below 2, with nothing else stored. Any other leading byte, or a 0 or 1 record with a fourth parameter of 2 or more, returns 0x8000000000000002.

name: ec_write_command_port
comment: Two byte arguments: CL selects the port pair (0x60 selects status port 0x64, anything else selects 0x66) and DL is the byte to write. It polls the selected status port for bit 1 clear with a 15-count delay (0x8B0) per turn and a 0x20000-iteration budget, checked both before the first delay and again after the loop, then does out on the status port with the value from DL. Returns 0 when the byte was written, or 0x8000000000000007 (EFI_TIMEOUT) if the budget runs out, in which case nothing is written.

name: write_port_66_wait_d1_clear
comment: Takes the low byte of its second argument as a value. It reads I/O port 0x66 and, while bit 1 is set, calls the 0xc00 delay with 15 and re-reads the port, giving up after 0x20000 iterations by returning 0x8000000000000007. Otherwise it writes the byte to I/O port 0x66 and returns 0.

name: find_config_table_entry
comment: It returns the pointer cached at 0x840 whenever that is nonzero, and otherwise reads the count at [0x820 + 0x68] and the base pointer at [0x820 + 0x70], walks that array in 0x18-byte steps comparing each record's first two qwords against the 16-byte constant at 0x7a0, and returns the third qword (record + 0x10) of the first match, caching it at 0x840. A zero count or no match leaves 0x840 zero and returns 0. The cache is never invalidated, so a second call returns the first match without re-walking - which is what 0x32C's two back-to-back calls rely on, except that when the first call found nothing the second repeats the whole walk. What the records describe is not decoded here.

name: MemOcGpio
comment: Runs only when MemoryOverClockSwitch == 1, and only if CpuSetup.OverclockingSupport == 1. The tables at RVA 0x1550 (17 entries) and 0x1750 (15 entries) are Intel's GPIO_GROUP_INFO for CNL/CML-H and -LP PCHs (0x1E bytes each: PID, PadOwn, HostOwn, GpiIs, GpiIe, GpiGpeSts, GpiGpeEn, SmiSts, SmiEn, NmiSts, NmiEn, PadCfgLock, PadCfgLockTx, PadCfgOffset, PadPerGroup). The H/LP choice (0x1100) is the 00:1F.0 device ID: 0x068x/0xA30x -> H, 0x028x/0x9D8x -> LP. Group 1 of the H table is PID 0x6E, PadCfg 0x790, 26 pads: GPP_B. PCR MMIO is 0xFD000000 | PID << 16 | offset (SBREG_BAR); the TX-lock change goes through the P2SB sideband registers at 00:1F.1 (0x1270) with opcode 0x13, the value Intel's reference code names GpioLockUnlock. Nothing in this module drives the pad low when the switch is 0. What GPP_B22 is wired to on this board is not known from the BIOS; a DIMM voltage select would fit the "memory overclock" name, and is only that: a guess, untested.

name: wait_controller_input_buffer_empty
comment: Polls the status port - 0x64 when the argument is 0x60, otherwise 0x66 - until bit 1 (input buffer full) is clear, calling 0x830 with 15 on each iteration. Returns 0 when the bit clears, or 0x8000000000000007 once the loop counter reaches 0x20000.

name: flush_data_port_to_80
comment: Picks the command port 0x64 (first byte argument 0x60) or 0x66 as 0x598 does, then while that port's bit 0 is set reads the data port 0x60 or 0x62, writes that byte to I/O port 0x80, and calls 0x890 with 5000 before polling again, up to 0x20000 times. Returns 0, or 0x8000000000000007 on timeout.

name: poll_status_bit1_then_write
comment: The first argument picks the port pair: with 0x60 in CL it polls bit 1 of port 0x64, otherwise bit 1 of port 0x66 (the decompiled C has this as 0x66 either way, which the cmovnz at 0x62B settles). It delays 15 units and re-polls up to 0x20000 times, then writes the second argument to the port it was polling, and returns 0; if the bit never cleared it returns 0x8000000000000007 instead. Every call site passes 0x62 in CL and uses the write to select an index on the same pair.

name: write_port_byte_after_wait
comment: Waits until bit 1 (0x02) of I/O port 0x64, or of 0x66 when the first argument is not 0x60, reads clear - 15-unit delays through 0x9B4 between reads, bounded at 0x20000 iterations - and then writes the byte from the second argument to that same port, returning 0. On exhaustion it returns 0x8000000000000007 without writing. What answers on I/O ports 0x60, 0x64, 0x66 and 0x80 is not identified in this module.

name: drain_port_62_into_80_wait_d0
comment: Reads I/O port 0x66 and, while bit 0 is set, reads a byte from I/O port 0x62, writes that byte to I/O port 0x80, delays via 0xc00 with 5000, and re-reads port 0x66. After 0x20000 iterations it returns 0x8000000000000007 instead of 0. The 0x62 to 0x80 transfer and the meaning of the two ports are not documented in this repository.

name: ec_drain_obf
comment: One byte argument, CL, selects the pair (0x60 gives status 0x64 and data 0x60, anything else gives status 0x66 and data 0x62). While the status port has bit 0 set it reads the data port, writes that byte to I/O port 0x80 or 0x7E, the port 0x1E above the data port it just read, waits 0x1388 (5000) counts through 0x8B0, and re-reads the status; the loop is bounded at 0x20000 iterations. Returns 0 or 0x8000000000000007 (EFI_TIMEOUT). The drained bytes are only echoed to 0x80/0x7E, so what they mean is not decided here.

name: send_command_data_pair
comment: Runs 0x5E4 (wait for the input buffer to empty), 0x55C (drain the output buffer), 0x4E4 (OUT the command byte), 0x5E4 again, an inline poll of the status port until bit 1 is clear, an OUT of the third argument to the data port, and 0x55C once more. Both the status port and the data port are chosen by comparing the first argument against the second (the command byte) rather than against 0x60; since no caller in this module passes a command byte of 0x60 or 0x62 they always resolve to 0x66 and 0x62. Only the opening 0x5E4 result is propagated - the inline poll and the closing 0x55C return values are discarded - so the 0x8000000000000007 timeout comes from that first wait alone, and if the inline poll times out the data byte is not written.

name: write_port_byte_after_wait
comment: Waits until bit 1 (0x02) of I/O port 0x64, or of 0x66 when the first byte argument is not 0x60, reads clear, with 15-unit delays through 0x00000a04 between reads and a 0x20000-iteration bound, and then writes the byte from the second argument to that same port, returning 0. On exhaustion it returns 0x8000000000000007 without writing. The device behind I/O ports 0x60, 0x62, 0x64 and 0x66 is not identified in this listing, so no mechanism is assigned to these accesses.

name: find_config_table_entry_by_guid
comment: It returns the pointer cached at 0x910 whenever that is non-zero. On a miss it reads the count at [0x8E8 + 0x68] and the base pointer at [0x8E8 + 0x70], walks that array in 0x18-byte steps comparing the first two qwords of each entry against the 16 bytes at 0x850 and 0x858, and caches the third qword of the first match (entry + 0x10) at 0x910, returning it; a zero count or no match leaves the cache zero and returns 0. It relies on 0x8E8, which only 0x0000032C sets, and the cache is never invalidated, so a second call returns the first match without re-walking - which is what 0x0000032C's two back-to-back calls rely on, except that a first call which found nothing repeats the whole walk. The 0x18-byte record shape (a 16-byte GUID then a pointer) and the +0x68/+0x70 offsets match EFI_CONFIGURATION_TABLE and the NumberOfTableEntries and ConfigurationTable members of the standard X64 EFI_SYSTEM_TABLE, which is the most likely identity of the structure at 0x8E8, but the GUID compared against is not decoded here.

name: OcRecovery
comment: The overclocking-recovery path, taken when the caller read EC 0x0741 bit 7 (EC_0741_OC_RECOVERY) set. Gets CpuSetup (0x2BB bytes, gCpuSetupGuid b08f97ff-...) and UniWillVariable (0xB4 bytes, UniWillVariable 9f33f85c-...), writes 1 to Uwv+0x5C (OverClockRecoveryFlag; GCUService shows a notice and clears it) and 0 to CpuSetup+0x1B7 ("OverClocking Feature"), and sets both variables back. Clearing the EC bit is the caller's job, immediately after this returns. The two offsets are read off the decompiler's stack layout of the two GetVariable buffers, not from a struct definition the module carries.

name: format_string_and_store_by_id
comment: Formats a string and passes it on. It first copies its third and fourth register arguments (R8 and R9) into its own incoming home slots, then builds the text in a 0x400-byte stack buffer with 0x0001c184, called as (buffer, 0x400, 0x140, fourth argument, address of the fourth argument) - the argument shape EDK2's AsciiSPrint-style formatter has, though that callee is only identified here by its address. It then calls 0x00021068 with (first argument, the second argument truncated to 16 bits from DX, the buffer). Its fifth, sixth and seventh arguments are supplied by the callers but never read by this function, and nothing here says what 0x140 or 0x00021068 do with the result.

name: wait_port_66_d1_clear
comment: Polls I/O port 0x66 in a loop: while bit 1 is set it delays via 0xc00 with 15 and reads the port again, giving up and returning 0x8000000000000007 after 0x20000 iterations, and returning 0 once the bit is clear. It writes no port and touches no memory.

name: drain_data_port_byte
comment: With 0x60 in CL it polls bit 0 of port 0x64, otherwise bit 0 of port 0x66, and while that bit is set it reads the data port (0x60 for that same base, 0x62 otherwise), writes the byte it read to port 0x80, delays 5000 units through 0x90C, and reads the status again. The poll counter is capped at 0x20000, after which it returns 0x8000000000000007; otherwise 0. What port 0x80 does with the byte is not decoded here.

name: wait_port_ready_bit
comment: Polls port 0x64 (first byte argument 0x60) or 0x66 until bit 1 reads as zero, calling 0x890 with 15 between polls and giving up after 0x20000 iterations. Returns 0 when the bit clears and 0x8000000000000007 on the cap. Identical to 0x598 apart from the missing final write.

name: ec_wait_ibf_clear
comment: Its single byte argument CL selects the status port (0x60 gives 0x64, anything else gives 0x66) and it does nothing else: it polls bit 1 for clear with a 15-count delay (0x8B0) per turn, bounded at 0x20000 iterations by checks before the first delay and after the loop, and returns 0 or 0x8000000000000007 (EFI_TIMEOUT). It is 0x5B8 without the final port write.

name: write_port_62_between_d1_polls
comment: Calls the 0x68c poll and returns its negative result unchanged if it failed. Otherwise it calls 0x630, then 0x5cc with the byte from its second argument (so the byte is written to I/O port 0x66), calls 0x68c again, and repeats the bit-1 poll inline; if that poll completes within 0x20000 iterations it writes the byte from its third argument to I/O port 0x62. It then calls 0x630 again and returns the value from the first 0x68c call. The guard around the 0x62 write uses EBP, which is caller-saved across the intervening calls and is not reloaded from 0x20000 after them.

name: drain_data_port_to_port_80
comment: While bit 0 (0x01) of I/O port 0x64, or of 0x66 when the first byte argument is not 0x60, is set, reads the byte from I/O port 0x62 (0x60 when that argument is 0x60), writes it to I/O port 0x80, and delays 5000 units through 0x00000a04 before re-reading the status port. Returns 0 once the bit clears, or 0x8000000000000007 when the 0x20000-iteration bound is reached.

name: send_three_command_data_pairs
comment: Takes its data byte in R9B and issues three 0x648 transactions on the 0x62 data / 0x66 status port pair: command 0xA3 with data 0x07, command 0xA2 with data 0x8C, and command 0xA5 with the R9B byte. A failure in either of the first two returns that status immediately; only the third call's status is conditionally moved into the return register. The command bytes 0xA3, 0xA2 and 0xA5 and the constants 0x07 and 0x8C are written literally and their meaning is not decoded anywhere in this module.

name: poll_status_bit1
comment: Reads the status port that the argument selects, 0x64 when it is 0x60 and 0x66 otherwise, and while bit 1 is set delays 15 units through 0x90C and reads the port again, up to 0x20000 times. Returns 0 once the bit is clear and 0x8000000000000007 if the counter runs out. It is the same bounded wait that 0x614 performs before its write, without the write.

name: ec_write_command_data
comment: Three byte arguments: CL selects the port pair, DL is the command byte and R8 the data byte. It runs 0x6B8 (wait for bit 1 clear), 0x630 (drain bit 0), 0x5B8 (write DL to the command port), 0x6B8 again, an inline bit-1 poll built from the same instructions as 0x5B8's with the same 15-count delay and 0x20000 budget, then an out of R8 to the data port, then 0x630 again; only the first wait's status is returned, and a timeout in the second wait just skips the data write. Where the .c and the listing disagree: the ports for this second half are chosen by comparing the CL argument with the DL command byte, equal giving status 0x64 and data 0x60 and otherwise status 0x66 and data 0x62, not by comparing CL against 0x60 as the .c reads. The caller at 0x438 passes CL = 0x62 with DL = 0xA3 and 0xA2, so the 0x66/0x62 pair is the one it uses.

name: wait_port_input_buffer_empty
comment: Polls bit 1 (0x02) of I/O port 0x64, or of 0x66 when the first argument is not 0x60, delaying 15 units through 0x9B4 between reads until the bit clears. Returns 0 on success, or 0x8000000000000007 once the 0x20000-iteration bound is reached.

name: write_byte_to_status_port_after_poll
comment: Picks the port as 0x64 when the first byte argument is 0x60 and 0x66 otherwise, polls bit 1 (0x02) of it until it reads clear - delaying 15 units through 0x00000a28 between reads, with a 0x20000-iteration bound - and then writes the byte from the second argument to that same port and returns 0. On exhaustion it returns 0x8000000000000007 without writing. 0x00000438 calls it with (0x62, 0xa4) and 0x00000894 calls it with the selector and byte it was given, so in this module it writes only to 0x66.

name: allocate_pages
comment: Rounds the byte count in RDX up to 4 KiB pages - pages = (size >> 12) + (size & 0xFFF != 0) - and calls the boot service at +0x28 (AllocatePages) with memory type 1 (EfiBootServicesData) and a memory-address in/out parameter preloaded with 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, the highest 64-bit physical address. A negative status zeroes the caller's out-pointer and returns 0x8000000000000009; otherwise the allocated physical address is stored through that pointer and the status is returned unchanged.

name: find_table_entry_by_id
comment: Returns the cached pointer at 0x8E0 whenever it is non-zero. On a cache miss it walks the array at [<pointer saved at 0x8D0> + 0x70] for the count read at [+0x68] entries of 0x18 bytes, comparing the first two qwords of each entry against the 16 bytes at 0x880 and 0x888, and on a match caches and returns the entry's third qword (offset +0x10). Returns 0 if the count is zero or nothing matches. The identifier stored at 0x880 and the structure 0x8D0 points at are not decoded here.

name: wait_port_input_buffer_empty
comment: Polls bit 1 (0x02) of I/O port 0x64, or of 0x66 when the first byte argument is not 0x60, delaying 15 units through 0x00000a04 between reads until the bit clears. Returns 0 on success, or 0x8000000000000007 once the 0x20000-iteration bound is reached.

name: write_index_data_byte
comment: The arguments are the port base (every call site passes 0x62), the index byte and the value. It waits for the status bit with 0x714, drains the data port with 0x68C, writes the index to the status port through 0x614, waits again, then waits for bit 1 of the data port to clear and writes the value to it: to 0x62 normally, or to 0x60 when the index byte itself is 0x62, which is the case in which the status port shifts to 0x64. It finishes by draining the data port again through 0x68C and returns the first wait's result unchanged, so the value is written even when the caller ignores the return. Whether this port pair addresses a device of any particular kind is not decoded in this repository.

name: exchange_command_and_data_byte
comment: Waits with 0x720, drains with 0x698, writes the second argument to the status port through 0x620, waits again, and only then writes the third argument to the data port. The status port is 0x64 when the first argument is 0x60 (in the three callees) or when the first two arguments are equal (in this function's own inline poll), and 0x66 otherwise; the data port is 0x60 when the first two arguments are equal and 0x62 otherwise. The inline poll before the second write watches bit 1 of the status port with the same 15-unit delays and 0x20000 bound and skips the write on exhaustion; the status from the first wait is what the function returns.

name: ec_write_port_byte
comment: Waits for bit 1 of the status byte at I/O port 0x66 (0x64 when the first argument is 0x60) to clear, polling up to 0x20000 times with a 15-microsecond delay between reads, then writes the second argument to that same port. Returns 0, or 0x8000000000000007 (negative when read as a signed value) once the poll count is exhausted.

name: mem_move_bytes
comment: memmove with the destination in the first parameter, the source in the second and the length in the third: when the source lies below the destination and the two ranges overlap it sets the direction flag and copies from the ends, otherwise forward. When the length and the distance between the two pointers are both at least 8 it first moves the bytes needed to bring both pointers to the same offset modulo 8, then copies length>>3 qwords with rep movsq and the remaining length&7 bytes with rep movsb. The flags pushed at entry are popped at the exit, so the direction flag set for a backward copy is restored to its original value, and the original destination is returned in RAX.

name: SyncOcVariables
comment: The menu gate. Setup[0x7D7] is question 0xEC6 in the IFR; the vendor Advanced form 0x2712 shows Ref "Memory" -> form 0x27B1 "Memory Overclocking Menu" only when 0xEC6 == 1 and CpuSetup[0x1B7] != 0, so Setup.Oem7D7 = UniWillVariable.MemoryOverClockSwitch (+0x33) is what un-suppresses the menu link. If the switch is 1, MemOcGpio (0x5D8) runs. If UniWillVariable.ApExistFlag (+0x5D) is 1, the Control Center's CPU core-voltage values are copied into the Intel OC knobs: ICpuCoreVoltageOffsetRangeType (+0x66) selects case 0 -> prefix 0 and ICpuCoreVoltageOffsetValue (+0x3A) -> CpuSetup+0x1BD; case 1 -> prefix 1 and ICpuCoreVoltageOffsetNegativeValue (+0x64) -> CpuSetup+0x1BD; case 2 -> the same as case 1 unless the negative value is 0, in which case as case 0. CoreVoltageOffsetPrefix is CpuSetup+0x1BF, and ICpuCoreVoltageValue (+0x34) goes to CpuSetup+0x1C0 "Core Voltage" in all three cases. Finally the ranges the service reads back as its slider limits are written: ICpuCoreVoltageMaximum = 2000, ICpuCoreVoltageMinimum = 0, ICpuCoreVoltageOffsetMaximum = 100, ICpuCoreVoltageOffsetMinimum = 0, as two 32-bit stores so the adjacent minimums become 0. evidence/uefi/2026-09-23-MemoryOverClockSwitch-set.txt shows 0x36 = 0x07D0 and 0x3C = 0x0064 in a variable this code wrote. CpuSetup is 0x2BB, UniWillVariable 0xB4, Setup 0x7D8 bytes.

name: poll_protocol_handles
comment: Calls the boot service at +0x140 (LocateProtocol) for the GUID at 0x2210 into a local, then +0x138 (LocateHandleBuffer) with search type 2 and the GUID at 0x21E0; for each handle it calls +0x98 (HandleProtocol) for the same GUID and then that interface's function at offset 0x10 with seven arguments, the second a 16-byte constant {0x22D85435, 0x43DBF24A, 0x5601047D, 0xB121DF06} assembled on the stack, stopping when the call returns 0 and keeping the last interface fetched. It frees the handle buffer through +0x48 (FreePool) and returns if no interface was kept or if the last call returned non-zero. Otherwise it loops on the kept interface's function at offset 0x18, called with the same constant, the byte 0x19 and three out-pointers: a negative status ends the loop, and on a non-negative one it calls the qword at offset 0 of the interface located at the start, passing the pointer that method wrote, the dword four bytes into that pointer, and a zeroed local, ending the loop when that indirect call returns non-zero. What either GUID names and what either method does is not decoded further.

name: find_table_entry_by_guid
comment: Returns the cached pointer at 0xAB0 when it is non-NULL. Otherwise it walks the array whose element count is at [cached structure + 0x68] and whose base is at [cached structure + 0x70] in 0x18-byte steps, comparing the first two qwords of each entry against the module constants at 0xA40 and 0xA48; on a match it caches and returns the third qword of that entry, at offset +0x10. The constants it matches on and the table it walks are not decoded further here.

name: delay_counter_ticks
comment: Splits its 32-bit argument into a repeat count (bits 22-31) and a tick count (bits 0-21) and performs repeat-count-plus-one passes. Each pass adds the tick count to the low 24 bits read from I/O port 0x1808 and then spins on repeated reads of that port, calling 0x260 to PAUSE, until bit 23 of (start + ticks - current) is set - which is the 24-bit counter having advanced by the tick count. Returns nothing, and nothing here fixes what time one increment of that counter is worth.

name: exchange_command_and_data_byte
comment: Waits with 0x00000770, drains with 0x000006e8, writes the second byte argument to the status port through 0x00000670, waits again with 0x00000770, and only then writes the third argument to the data port, which is I/O port 0x62 when the first two byte arguments differ and 0x60 when they are equal. The inline poll before that data write watches bit 1 of I/O port 0x66 (0x64 when the two arguments are equal) with the same 15-unit delays and 0x20000 bound, but on exhaustion it skips the write instead of reporting an error. It drains once more with 0x000006e8 and returns the status of the first 0x00000770 call; the other helper results are not checked.

name: find_config_table_by_guid
comment: It returns the vendor-table pointer cached at 0xB20 whenever that global is non-null, so only a first call with an empty cache does any work. That path takes the SystemTable cached at 0xB00, reads the entry count at +0x68 and the array pointer at +0x70, and walks the array in strides of 0x18, comparing each entry's first two qwords against the 8-byte constants at 0xA60 and 0xA68; on a match it reads the entry's third qword, at index*0x18+0x10, stores it in 0xB20 and returns it. With no match, or with a zero count, it returns 0. 0x32C calls it twice in a row and uses only the second result, the first being the call that fills the cache.

name: write_port_byte_after_wait
comment: Waits until bit 1 (0x02) of I/O port 0x64, or of 0x66 when the first argument is not 0x60, reads clear - 15-unit delays through 0x00000bdc, bounded at 0x20000 iterations - and then writes the byte from the second argument to that same port, returning 0. On exhaustion it returns 0x8000000000000007 without writing. The device behind I/O ports 0x60, 0x64, 0x66 and 0x80 is not identified in this module, so no mechanism is assigned to these accesses.

name: load_oc_state_from_protocol
comment: Locates the protocol at GUID 0x2570 and, if that succeeds, reads one 0x28-byte record out of it: the record index is the byte at +0xE3 and the fields copied are +4, +6, +8, +0xA (word), +0xC (word), +0xE, +0x10 (word), +0x12 (word), +0x16, +0x18, +0x1A, +0x1C, +0x1E, +0x20, +0x22 and +0x24, landing in the working globals 0x26E3, 0x26D0, 0x26D1, 0x26D2, 0x26D4, 0x26D6, 0x26D7, 0x26D9, 0x26DB, 0x26DE, 0x26DF, 0x26E0, 0x26DC, 0x26DD, 0x26E1 and 0x26E2. It also takes byte +0xE0 into 0x26CC, byte +0xE1 into 0x26CE, the word at +0xB0 + index*2 into 0x26C3 and byte +0xE5 into 0x2C5D. The call to 0xB94 sits on the failure path too, so it runs whether or not the protocol was located.

name: wait_status_port_bit1_clear
comment: Polls bit 1 (0x02) of I/O port 0x64, or of 0x66 when the first byte argument is not 0x60, delaying 15 units through 0x00000a28 between reads until the bit clears. It returns 0 on success, or 0x8000000000000007 once the 0x20000-iteration bound is reached, and writes no port and touches no memory. 0x00000894 brackets its two byte writes with this wait; 0x00000438 spells the same poll out inline.

name: wait_port_counter_ticks
comment: Splits its argument: bits 22 and above give a repeat count, bits 0-21 an offset. On each of count+1 passes it reads I/O port 0x1808, masks 24 bits, adds the offset, and spins through 0x2C0 until (target - value) has bit 23 set, i.e. until the counter has passed the target; the 0x400000 loaded into EDI inside the loop is never read again.

name: append_callback_node_to_list
comment: Allocates a 0x18-byte node through [0x29478+0x40] with pool type 4 and, on success, writes three fields: the function address 0x6d8 at +0x10, the sentinel address 0x2b380 at +0 and the current contents of the global 0x2b388 at +8. It then links the node in by setting the old tail's +0 to the new node and 0x2b388 to the new node, making 0x2b380/0x2b388 a self-referential list head. On allocation failure it returns without touching the list and without reporting a status - the caller's loop continues regardless.

name: find_config_table_by_guid
comment: Returns the cached pointer at 0xB58 whenever it is non-null. Otherwise it clears that cache and, if the count at [0xB30+0x68] is non-zero, walks the configuration table array at [0xB30+0x70] in 0x18-byte steps, comparing the first 16 bytes of each entry against the 16 bytes at 0xAA0 and 0xAA8 and caching the entry's third qword, the table pointer at +0x10, in 0xB58. It returns that cache, which is zero when no entry matched. The 0x18-byte stride and the 16-byte GUID followed by a pointer are the standard configuration table layout; the GUID being matched is not decoded here.

name: read_port_register_byte
comment: Makes two exchanges through 0x784 with the port selector 0x62 - the pair 0xA3/0x07, then the register byte from the third argument - writes 0xA4 to the status port through 0x620, then polls bit 0 of I/O port 0x66 until it is set (15-unit delays through 0x9B4, 0x20000 iterations, 0x8000000000000007 on exhaustion) and stores the byte read from I/O port 0x62 through the pointer in the fourth argument. The first two arguments are ignored. The three callers in 0x454 pass 0x40, 0x3C and 0x3D as that register byte; docs/findings.md section 8 reports this same 0xA3/0xA2/0xA4/0xA5-over-0x62 sequence as the vendor's EC RAM access, with OemOcDxe's 0x41 read mapping to EC RAM 0x0741, which would put this module's 0x40 read at 0x0740, PROJECT_ID in ec/annotations/registers.yaml - but the +0x700 base between the low byte sent here and the EC map is not visible in this listing, and findings.md calls that reading inferred rather than confirmed.

name: wait_port_1808_ticks
comment: The single 32-bit argument packs two fields: bits 22:0 (masked with 0x3FFFFF) is a count to wait and bits 31:22 is a repeat count, taken as the argument shifted right 0x16. For each repeat it reads I/O port 0x1808, masks the value to 24 bits, adds the count to make a target, and spins until (target - a fresh read) has bit 23 set, calling pause (0x2C0) on each turn except the first check; the loop is left when the 24-bit counter has passed the target, and it repeats one more time than the repeat field says because that field is tested after being decremented. The instruction loading EDI with 0x400000 at 0x87C is dead: the target is held in ESI and EDI is not read again.

name: find_record_by_8byte_id
comment: It reads a 64-bit count at [param+0x68] and a record array at [param+0x70], and walks that array in strides of 0x18, passing each record to 0x00000a34. It returns 0 when the count is zero or when no record matched, and otherwise the qword at record+0x10 of the first record that did. What the records describe is not decoded here.

name: ec_wait_ibf_clear
comment: The same status poll as 0x0000078C, waiting for bit 1 of the byte at port 0x66 (0x64 when the first argument is 0x60) to clear with 15-microsecond delays and a 0x20000-iteration limit, but it writes nothing. Returns 0 or 0x8000000000000007.

name: alloc_buffer_type4
comment: It zeroes a qword at RSP+0x38, then makes a three-argument indirect call through offset 0x40 of the table at 0x00000cf0 with ECX=4, the incoming value in EDX and RSP+0x38 as the out-pointer, and returns the qword the call left there. The call's own result is never tested, so a failing call yields 0. Every chain buffer in this module comes from here and none of those callers check for failure.

name: exchange_command_and_data_byte
comment: Waits for bit 1 of the status port with 0x00000830, drains with 0x000007a8, writes the byte from the second argument to that same port (0x66 here) through 0x00000730, waits again, and only then writes the byte from the third argument, which goes to I/O port 0x62 unless the first and second byte arguments are equal, in which case it goes to 0x60. The inline poll before that second write watches bit 1 of 0x66 (0x64 when the two arguments are equal) with the same 15-unit delays and 0x20000 bound, but on exhaustion it skips the write instead of reporting an error. It drains once more with 0x000007a8 and returns the status of the first 0x00000830 call; the other helpers' results are not checked. Its three call sites in 0x00000438 pass (0x62, 0xa3, 0x07), (0x62, 0xa2, 0x82) and (0x62, 0xa5, <the computed byte>), so the command byte lands on 0x66 and the payload on 0x62 in all three.

name: read_port_register_byte
comment: Ignores its first argument (CL is forced to 0x62) and uses the second byte argument as the data byte of the first exchange, with the third argument as the register byte carried by the second. It makes two 0x000007d4 exchanges, 0xa3 then 0xa2, each carrying one of those two bytes, writes 0xa4 to the status port through 0x00000670, then polls bit 0 of I/O port 0x66 until it is set, with 15-unit delays through 0x00000a04 and a 0x20000-iteration bound that returns 0x8000000000000007, and stores the byte read from I/O port 0x62 through the pointer in its fourth argument. A negative status from any step is returned without touching that pointer. Its two call sites in 0x00000494 pass 4 and 0x9f, and 7 and 0x51, as those second and third bytes, so the first exchange's data byte is a caller-supplied value rather than a constant.

name: delay_by_port_counter_ticks
comment: The argument packs two fields: bits 0 through 21 are a tick count and bits 22 through 31 a repeat count. The routine runs one more time than that repeat count, and each pass reads the 24-bit counter at I/O port 0x1808, adds the tick count to it, then spins calling the PAUSE helper at 0x2C0 until bit 23 of the difference between the target and a fresh read is set, which is the condition that the counter has moved past the target. The inner loop has no timeout of its own. The counter's frequency and what the callers are actually waiting for are not decoded here.

name: delay_microseconds
comment: It converts the argument to a count of the 24-bit counter at I/O port 0x1808 and hands that to 0x850: multiply by 0x369E99 (3579545), then divide by 1000000 through an unsigned 128-bit multiply by 0x431BDE82D7B634DB and a shift of 0x12 on top of the implicit 64, which is 3.579545 counts per microsecond, the scale EDK II's microsecond delay uses. It returns the argument unchanged in RAX. The module passes 0xF (15) and 0x1388 (5000) to it, and 0x32C uses the raw count 0x16B against port 0x1808 itself rather than converting.

name: sum_chain_record_lengths
comment: It returns 0 for a NULL pointer. Otherwise it walks a record chain, reading a 16-bit length from bytes 2 and 3 of each record (byte 3 shifted left 8 plus byte 2), adding it to a running total, and advancing the cursor by that length alone; it stops and returns the total when byte 0 of the record is zero or the length is zero. A record whose byte 0 is 0x7f and byte 1 is 0xff ends the walk and returns the total plus 4. Why the cursor advances by the length with no fixed prefix while the terminator case adds 4 is not resolved here.

name: wait_port_input_buffer_empty
comment: Polls bit 1 (0x02) of I/O port 0x64, or of 0x66 when the argument is not 0x60, delaying 15 units through 0x00000bdc between reads until the bit clears. Returns 0 on success, or 0x8000000000000007 once the 0x20000-iteration bound is reached.

name: find_config_table_entry_by_guid
comment: Cached lookup: when the global at 0xC00 is non-zero it is returned unchanged, otherwise the array at offset 0x70 of the pointer cached at 0xBE0 is walked in 0x18-byte steps, bounded by the count at its offset 0x68, comparing the 16 bytes at each entry's offsets 0 and 8 against the bytes at 0xB60 and 0xB68 and caching the matching entry's qword at +0x10 in 0xC00. It returns 0 when the count is 0 or when no entry matches, and in the miss case it caches that 0, so the next call walks again. The 0x18-byte entries are a 16-byte identifier followed by a pointer, which is the shape of the EFI system configuration table, but the identity of the bytes at 0xB60 is not in this listing.

name: ec_write_command_data
comment: Waits for the status bit to clear (0x0000088C), drains pending status (0x00000804), writes the second argument to port 0x66, waits again, writes the third argument to port 0x62, and drains a second time, returning the first wait's result. The two port selections compare the first argument against the second rather than against 0x60, so unless those two happen to be equal the status port is 0x66 and the data port 0x62.

name: classify_cpu_signature
comment: Calls the CPUID wrapper at 0x2B0 with leaf 1 and four out-pointers, takes the EAX result, masks it with 0x0FFF0FF0, and compares the result against 0x806E0, 0x906E0, 0xA0650 and 0xA0660. Each of those groups is then qualified against a list of values read from the word at 0xE0000002, and a match writes a small code into BL: 0, 1, 2 or 3 depending on the group, with 4 left in BL from the function entry when nothing matches. Returns AL. The meaning of the four codes, and of the word at 0xE0000002, is not decoded here.

name: scale_units_to_port_ticks
comment: Multiplies the argument by 0x369E99, which is 3579545, and then by the 64-bit constant 0x431BDE82D7B634DB, keeping the high half of the 128-bit product and shifting right 18; that is an exact unsigned division yielding 3579545 ticks per 1000000 units of the argument, so 15 gives 53 and 5000 gives 17897. The result is passed straight to the tick delay at 0x8AC, and the original argument is returned unchanged. Nothing in the listing establishes what unit the argument is in; every call site passes a small literal.

name: wait_and_write_status_port
comment: Chooses port 0x64 when its first argument's low byte is 0x60 and 0x66 otherwise, then polls the byte at that port until bit 1 (0x02) is clear, delaying 15 units through 0xD04 on each iteration. It gives up after 0x20000 iterations with 0x8000000000000007 (EFI_TIMEOUT). On success it writes its second argument back to that same port (0x64 or 0x66) and returns 0, so this is not a read and a write on a separate data port.

name: build_string_from_runs
comment: Zeroes ten bytes of stack scratch through 0x260, then appends eight run-length runs to it: run i writes the byte at 0x2691+i from the previous length to the current one, taking the lengths from the bytes at 0x2803 and then 0x2804 through 0x280A as cumulative end offsets rather than as sizes. The first eight bytes of the result go to 0x2300 and the last two to 0x2308, so the output is one ten-byte string. Nothing checks the total length (0x280A) against the ten bytes that were cleared, and what the eight source bytes and the length bytes stand for is not decoded further.

name: find_config_table_entry_by_guid
comment: Cached lookup: when the global at 0x00000c78 is non-zero it is returned unchanged, otherwise the global is zeroed and the array at offset 0x70 of the structure cached at 0x00000c50 is walked in 0x18-byte steps, bounded by the count at offset 0x68, comparing the 16 bytes at each entry's offsets 0 and 8 against the bytes at 0x00000bb0 and 0x00000bb8 and caching the qword at +0x10 of the match. Returns 0 when the count is zero or nothing matches. Offsets 0x68 and 0x70 are where NumberOfTableEntries and ConfigurationTable sit in EFI_SYSTEM_TABLE, and 0x00000310 passes its second argument to 0x00000388 as the structure cached at 0x00000c50, but nothing here identifies the 16 bytes at 0x00000bb0 and 0x00000bb8 that are being searched for.

name: poll_status_bit1_until_clear
comment: Chooses I/O port 0x64 when the low byte of the argument equals 0x60 and port 0x66 otherwise, reads a byte from it, and while bit 1 is set calls 0xb3c with 15, re-reads the port and increments a counter, stopping when the bit clears or the counter reaches 0x20000. Returns 0 when the bit clears and 0x8000000000000007 when the count limit is hit. What the two ports are is not established in this module.

name: exchange_command_and_data_byte
comment: Waits with 0x000008e8, drains with 0x00000860, writes the second argument to the status port through 0x000007e8, waits again, and only then writes the third argument to the data port, which is I/O port 0x62 when the first two arguments differ and 0x60 when they are equal. The inline poll before that write watches bit 1 of I/O port 0x66 (0x64 when the arguments are equal) with the same 15-unit delays and 0x20000 bound, but on exhaustion it skips the write instead of reporting an error. The three helper results are not checked; the value returned is the one from the first 0x000008e8 call.

name: find_guid_in_18byte_record_array
comment: Returns the pointer cached at 0x00000ca0 when that global is non-zero. Otherwise it zeroes the global and, if the count at [0x00000c78]+0x68 is non-zero, walks the array at [0x00000c78]+0x70 in 0x18-byte steps, comparing each entry's qwords at +0 and +8 against the constants at 0x00000bf0 and 0x00000bf8, and caches and returns the entry's qword at +0x10; it returns 0 when the count is zero or nothing matches. The 0x18 stride and the 16-byte-key/pointer layout match EFI_CONFIGURATION_TABLE, but the standard EFI_SYSTEM_TABLE carries NumberOfTableEntries at +0x58 and ConfigurationTable at +0x60, not at +0x68 and +0x70, so the structure cached at 0x00000c78 is not identified here and the 16 bytes being searched for are not decoded.

name: write_value_to_named_record
comment: Calls 0x76c with the table, count and name from its first three arguments, forcing the selector argument to 3 so the delimiter byte is 0x08, and passes a four-qword output structure on the stack. If the lookup returns a negative status it returns that. Otherwise it reads the type byte at output+0x10 and stores its fourth argument through that address: a byte for 0x00 and 0x0a, a word for 0x0b, a dword for 0x0c and a qword for 0x0e. Types 0x00 and 0x01 additionally require the value to be below 2; every other type byte returns 0x8000000000000002. The write goes back into the table the caller passed, so this modifies the table in place.

name: flush_output_buffer_to_port_80
comment: Picks the same 0x64/0x66 status port from its argument's low byte, then while status bit 0 (0x02 masked as 0x01) is set reads the byte at 0x60 or 0x62 and writes it to I/O port 0x80, delaying 5000 units through 0xD04 between bytes; the port for the read is chosen by the same test, while the output port is always 0x80 because ECX is unconditionally set to 0x62 before the 0x1E offset is added.
